To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the directory structure can be used to predict the evolution of Web sites and that a data mining-driven Web archiving technique can be devised to improve efficiency.

(a) the number of pages in a directory structure is an effective predictor of the number of pages inserted to/removed  from the directory; (b) the number of inserted/removed pages is an effective predictor for the number of pages that need to be downloaded; and (c) the number of downloaded pages is an effective proxy to the number of changed pages.
the proposed NEAR-Miner is able to identify the directories that have undergone significant evolution with high precision and recall.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions. (i) How can we identify the directories that are likely to have changed significantly since the last crawl? (ii) How can we efficiently and reliably identify such directories? (iii) How can we use these identified directories to guide the (re)crawling process to minimize the amount of pages that have to be downloaded and maintained in a Web archive?
two main questions: (1) How can we identify the most significant directories in a large Web site?

there is a significant need for the development of new tools and techniques to facilitate the management of large Web archive collections.

the NEAR-Miner is an effective and efficient tool for identifying directories that have changed significantly and thus need to be re-visited and re-crawled by a crawler.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have designed an efficient Web archiving technique that is based on mining the Web directories for the purpose of maintaining Web archives.

we propose a new method for identifying directories in a Web archive which are likely to have changed since the previous crawl, and we propose a method to identify pages in the directories that are likely to have been inserted or deleted.
we are able to mine the evolution of Web sites and identify directories that are most likely to change in the future.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evolution of Web sites can be modeled as a graph of associations of directories and pages, where the evolution of the graph is a result of insertions and removals of directories and pages.
the directory structure of Web pages is an effective predictor of change.
the directory structure can be exploited for efficiently maintaining Web archives by identifying directories that are likely to have changed significantly and (re)downloaded.
